newsitem.title: FRANCE: AUGIN EXPECTED TO CROSS FINISHING LINE ON MONDAY.
newsitem.headline: AUGIN EXPECTED TO CROSS FINISHING LINE ON MONDAY.

text.p: Up to 70,000 people were expected in the small west France coastal resort of Les-Sables-d'Olonne on Monday for the arrival of the leader in the round-the-world solo Vendee Globe sailing race, organisers said on Sunday.
Christophe Auguin, aboard his vessel Geodis, was expected to cross the finishing line at about 0930 local (0830 GMT), they said.
"Thousands of people are already arriving and we expect between 50,000 and 70,000 people will be present," a race spokeswoman told Reuters.
Auguin will therefore reach Les-Sables-d'Olonne in 106 days, breaking the 109-day race record set in 1989 by another French sailor, Titouan Lamazou.
The other competitors are hundreds of miles behind him.
The race has been marked by dramatic rescues and the disappearance of a competitor.
The accident-prone third Vendee Globe Challenge, through lonely, towering seas fraught with dangerous icebergs, has confirmed its reputation as one of the world's most dangerous sports events.

Only seven of the 16 competitors are still in the race which skirts southern Africa, rounds Antarctica clockwise towards Cape Horn to end in Les Sables d'Olonne, on France's Atlantic coast, where it started on November 3.
Canadian Gerry Roufs has been missing for over a month. He was last in contact with organisers when in a remote Antarctic area between New Zealand and Cape Horn in some of the world's heaviest seas.
Two other competitors, Frenchman Thierry Dubois and Briton Tony Bullimore, were plucked from the sea by the Australian navy in dramatic rescues after their boats capsized southwest of Australia.
Another Frenchman, Raphael Dinelli, was rescued by fellow competitor Pete Goss and taken to Tasmania.
Most other competitors had to make for land after breaking equipment in collisions with unidentified objects or animals. Some of them, although disqualified, have resumed the race.
The accidents, and the costly and risky rescues, have triggered charges that the French-organised race was too dangerous and that yacht builders had sacrificed safety to speed.
